To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the successor representation (a) is an intermediate between model-based and model-free reinforcement learning, and (b) is a plausible mechanism underlying semi-flexible choice.

(i) the human brain computes a successor representation, (ii) the successor representation is more efficient than model-based reinforcement learning, and (iii) the successor representation has the unique property of being sensitive to changes in the environment but not in the task structure.

1) humans can learn to choose actions in a semi-flexible way, 2) the semi-flexible learning system is best described by a computational model that we call the ‘successor representation,’ 3) the successor representation is distinct from both model-based and model-free systems, and 4) the successor representation can be used to predict how human behavior adapts to changing environments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature and neural implementation of human reward learning.
how humans make choices.
the computational mechanisms that underlie learning, memory, and decision-making in human cognition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the authors have provided a novel and interesting computational model of human reward learning and provided evidence for it.
the successor representation (SR) is an intermediate mechanism that combines the advantages and disadvantages of the two dominant mechanisms.
the successor representation provides a plausible and empirically supported account for a range of cognitive phenomena that cannot be explained by either the model-free or model-based accounts alone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the successor representation, an algorithm that stores partially computed action values, is a computational substrate of semi-flexible choice, introducing a more cognitive notion of habitual behavior in humans.
we show that a third, intermediate system is at least partly implemented in human reinforcement learning.
we provide a computational mechanism that can explain the flexibility of human choice and learning in a way that is more cognitively plausible than the two dominant models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
humans can learn to flexibly adjust their choices in a semi-automatic way.
the successor representation, as a third model, can explain a range of human data that the other two models cannot.
humans may use a more flexible, semi-habitual mechanism to guide their choices.
